Hi Zach,

I think Vince is right in that sed or perl is the traditional/efficient way to parse large amounts sequence data. 

If you are set on R, grep and regex should be able get you where you need to go (depending on the size of the task).

Its not clear from the question what exactly the data.frame you want looks like (eg what are the rows and what are the columns?).
 Assuming you want something like column1 = id and column 2 = sequence, heres how I would do it:

# test.txt is the text file containing data. This loads it as a vector with one line of data per 'slot'.
d <- readLines('test.txt')
head(d)
 
# identify all characters between an '@' or '+' at the beginning of a line and the sequence 'read_id=';replace with either + or @
d <- gsub( pattern = '(^@|^[+]).*?read_id=', replacement = '\\1', x = d )
 
# remove the barcode tag
d <- gsub( pattern = 'barcode=CGGCATAT', replacement = '', x = d)
 
# reform into a data.frame
ids <- grep('(^@|^[+])', d) #indices of 'ids'
my.df <- data.frame ( id = d[ids], sequence = d[-ids])
head(my.df)

Created by Pretty R at inside-R.org

Hope this helps --

Steve

parts:
Hey Zach,

It seems like most of what you're wanting to do is probably better done in Bash using tools like sed instead of R (although as Steve indicated, there are some R functions that might get you equivalent results). To add to what Vince just said, I would probably accomplish this task using a for loop in a Bash script something like so (although this may not be the most elegant or fastest solution):


#!/bin/bash
set -eu

for file in 1 2 3

do

# Define input file and output file names
InputFile="Input"$file".fq"

OutputFile="Output"$file".fq"

# Perform your sed operations
sed 's/\([@\\+]\).*read_id=\([^\s]*\) .*$/\1\2/' $InputFile > $OutputFile

done


So assuming you execute this script from a directory containing the files "Input1.fq", "Input2.fq", and "Input3.fq", you would get back "Output1.fq", "Output2.fq", and "Output3.fq" which would have been modified using that sed command. You can of course modify the script according to the file names/file paths you actually have and the output files you want.

Hope that helps!
Evan

parts: I think the only issue is that:
for file in 1 2 3

is not very robust (what if you forget to type out a number?) and not dynamic (what if you add a new file and forget to change your script accordingly?). You can use find to propagate this list automatically, as long as you use a clear naming scheme. This is how I'd tackle it.

$ mkdir fastq_files output
$ cd fastq_files
$ touch {1..10}.fq # make test data
$ cd ..

Then save this (below) to process.sh and chmod u+x it:

#!/bin/bash
set -e
set -u
set -o pipefail

FILEKEY=$(basename $1 .fq) # strip data directory and extension

echo "processing file $FILEKEY"
sed 's/\([@\\+]\).*read_id=\([^\s]*\) .*$/\1\2/' fastq_files/${FILEKEY}.fq > output/${FILEKEY}_processed.fq

Note how we just use extension to match FASTQ files. You may wish to be less permissive, depending on your project structure, etc. Verify that these are indeed the same files you want to process.

Then we just pipe these names into xargs, which takes a single name (with the -n 1 option) and passes it to process.sh, with:

$ find fastq_files -name "*.fq" | xargs -n 1 ./process.sh

All output is saved with the suffix _processed.fq. The numbered FASTQ files were empty, so no results, but test_processed.fq verifies everything looks like it's working. This should be fast enough, but if you need to run it in parallel, you can use -P 10 or something with xargs. Hi Zach,

1) It printed the (correct) output in the terminal, but did not alter the file itself or produce a new output file.

Yes, this is expected. You never want to modify data in place. You should treat data as read-only, always. Why? What if an unexpected error occurred and it left your files destroyed? 

The right way to handle this is to redirect the standard output of sed to a file with >. For example:

$ sed 's/\([@\\+]\).*read_id=\([^\s]*\) .*$/\1\2/' test.fq > new_file.fq

2) I have a directory with multiple FASTQ files, named 81.fastq, 82. fastq, etc. I need to perform this function on every file in the directory. What's the best way to do this, instead of running the same function on each file individually?
